newsitem.title: USA: W.House's Yellen sees sustainable path for economy.
newsitem.headline: W.House's Yellen sees sustainable path for economy.

text.p: The U.S. economy is remaining on a sustainable growth path with no sign that inflation is on the rise, despite strong jobs growth, White House chief economist Janet Yellen said Friday.

Yellen, who recently left her post as a Federal Reserve governor to take up her position at the White House, saw strength in the latest figures from the Labor Department showing a 339,000 jump in February payrolls along with a drop in the unemployment rate to 5.3 percent from 5.4 percent.

"The American economy is a job-creating machine that is just having continued success creating new employment opportunities without any sign of generating inflation," Yellen told the U.S. cable television network CNBC.
She said there was no evidence in the February jobs report of wage gains exceeding productivity growth.
Asked about a statistic in the employment report on voluntary job leavers that some economists view as a gauge of labor market pressures, Yellen played down the number.
The report showed that the number of people leaving their jobs as a percentage of the unemployed fell in February to 10.9 percent from 12.3 percent in January.
"I personally wouldn't read much into monthly fluctuations in that statistic," Yellen said of the number, which some economists call the "quit rate." She noted the statistic is very volatile.
Still, she said a number of surveys and other measures indicate a great deal of confidence among workers in their ability to find jobs.

The White House official also said the concept of the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment -- the jobless rate below which inflationary pressures can develop -- was "very imprecise" because that number can vary depending on developments in the business cycle.
Yellen declined to comment on Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's cautionary remarks on the huge run-up in U.S. equity prices.

However, she said, "For my own part, I think that the current value of the stock market reflects the confidence that investors have about the good economic performance we have had and its ability to continue that way."
She pointed out that there are always risks and said the business cycle was probably not dead.
Yellen described labor markets as "quite tight" and said that policy makers were correct to watch that but stressed that she did not see evidence of growing inflationary pressures.
Turning to negotiations between the White House and Congress over the budget, Yellen said she was "very optimistic" and "very confident" that the talks would lead to a balanced budget.
